analysis.one_liner: Lets gun violence victims sue gun makers and dealers, ending the industry's lawsuit shield.
analysis.headline: The bill to end the gun industry's lawsuit shield died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or a vote, despite a Democratic House majority and 40 sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law — the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act — currently bars most lawsuits against gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for harm caused when a gun is later used in a crime. This bill would repeal that shield, so shooting victims and their families could sue the gun industry in state and federal courts like victims of other defective or negligently sold products. It would also make ATF gun-trace data usable as evidence in those lawsuits. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would regain the right to sue manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations when a gun was negligently or unlawfully sold; municipalities could also pursue claims. Courts would have access to federal gun-trace data, which is currently shielded from lawsuits, making it easier to prove how a crime gun reached the shooter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2-4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (15 U.S.C. 7901-7903), which currently prohibits civil suits against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.

Makes the ATF Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and discovery, and admissible as evidence, in any state or federal civil case or administrative proceeding — ending the special protection trace data now enjoys.
The bill's stated purpose is 'equal access to justice' — putting gun industry defendants in the same legal position as other product makers, who can be sued when their products injure people.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations would face civil lawsuits, discovery costs, and potential judgments for guns they sold, including suits over later criminal misuse. Small dealers argue they could be dragged into litigation even when they followed all laws and the harm came from a third party's crime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Repealing the shield would expose gun sellers to suits over the criminal acts of third parties, since the PLCAA bars claims based on 'criminal or unlawful misuse' of a firearm — sellers who complied with every law could still face expensive litigation and settlements.

The change applies retroactively to existing law with no statute of limitations adjustment, inviting a wave of litigation whose costs would fall on the industry and, critics argue, be passed to consumers through higher prices and fewer dealers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims, the bill restores a right almost every other consumer has: to hold a seller accountable in court when a product causes harm. The genuine cost is litigation burden on law-abiding dealers and the possibility of lawsuits over third-party crimes, which the gun industry argues punishes legal commerce. Whether that burden is excessive or simply the normal cost of accountability depends on how courts apply the restored liability rules — the bill itself offers no middle-ground carve-out for dealers who followed the law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Crime subcommittee two weeks later, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on June 11, 2019, joined by 39 Democratic cosponsors — all from his own party.
The House was run by a Democratic majority in this Congress, so the bill's own party controlled the committee and the floor schedule.
It was referred to the Judiciary Committee on June 11, 2019, and on June 28, 2019 to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations are better off: they keep the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shield that blocks most lawsuits over gun deaths and injuries, and trace data stays out of courts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers and dealers, who keep the shield

for.name: Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's civil liability shield and open ATF trace data to lawsuits.

for.name: 39 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in a Democratic House
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 11, 2019 and referred it to the Crime subcommittee; never held a markup or reported it to the floor.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed any repeal of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which the NRA helped win in 2005 and treats as a top legislative priority to preserve.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 supporters — the sponsor and 39 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote where broader splits could show up.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 2005 federal shield that exempts them from most lawsuits over deaths and injuries caused by guns they made and sold. Repeal would expose them to negligence and marketing suits for the first time in two decades.

industries.industry: Gun dealers, importers, and trade associations
industries.note: The current law protects them alongside manufacturers; the bill strips that protection too, and would let plaintiffs use ATF trace data to show how crime guns moved through the retail channel. The industry's interest in keeping the shield runs directly against victims' interest in suing.
Repeal would create a new field of civil litigation on behalf of shooting victims; their gain comes through the same lawsuits victims would file, so their interest runs alongside the public's here.
